issues.legal_issue: A claim to recover property conveyed by a natural guardian in a voidable transfer is governed by the limitation period for setting aside that transfer, rather than the period for possession based on title.
material_facts: A natural guardian conveyed the minor’s immovable property by sale deeds without obtaining the court’s permission.
The minor died before attaining majority.
The persons claiming through the minor filed suit more than three years after the minor’s death, seeking declaration and possession without setting aside the sale deeds.
issues.conclusion: The claim was governed by Article 60 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and was time-barred; Article 65 did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Article 60(b)(ii) of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a three-year period from the ward’s death for a suit to set aside a transfer made by the guardian when the ward dies before attaining majority. A suit seeking possession by avoiding a guardian’s transfer is, in substance, a suit to set aside that transfer, and Article 65 does not govern it. The Court relied on Madhukar Vishwanath v. Madahav and Narayan v. Babasaheb.

rule.if: minor_guardian_transfer_suit and transfer_made_by_natural_guardian and ward_died_before_majority and claim_filed_after_limitation

predicates.minor_guardian_transfer_suit: The proceeding is a claim to recover property transferred by a guardian of a minor.
predicates.transfer_made_by_natural_guardian: A natural guardian transferred the minor’s immovable property.
predicates.ward_died_before_majority: The minor died before reaching majority.
predicates.claim_filed_after_limitation: The persons claiming through the minor brought the claim after the applicable limitation period had elapsed.

issues.definition: When a claim to recover property transferred by a natural guardian is brought after the applicable limitation period has elapsed following the minor’s death before majority, the claim is time-barred.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for declaration and possession cannot avoid a registered sale by a natural guardian without first obtaining relief setting aside the sale.
material_facts: The natural guardian executed registered sale deeds that purported to convey the minor’s immovable property without prior court permission.
The plaintiffs sought declaration and possession but did not ask the court to set aside the sale deeds.
issues.conclusion: The sale deeds were voidable, not void, and had to be set aside before the plaintiffs could obtain relief concerning the properties; the suit as framed was not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 8(2) and 8(3) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, a disposal contrary to the statutory requirements is voidable at the instance of the minor or a person claiming under the minor. A voidable registered transfer remains effective until set aside, so a claim for possession cannot proceed without relief avoiding the transfer. The Court relied on Vishwambhar v. Laxminarayan and distinguished void transactions discussed in Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University.

rule.if: suit_for_declaration_and_possession and registered_transfer_by_natural_guardian and transfer_is_voidable and suit_does_not_seek_to_set_aside_transfer

predicates.suit_for_declaration_and_possession: The proceeding seeks a declaration of entitlement to property and recovery of possession.
predicates.registered_transfer_by_natural_guardian: A natural guardian conveyed the minor’s immovable property by registered instrument.
predicates.transfer_is_voidable: The transfer is effective unless avoided by a person entitled to challenge it.
predicates.suit_does_not_seek_to_set_aside_transfer: The claimant seeks relief concerning the property without asking the court to set aside the transfer.

issues.definition: A suit seeking declaration and possession is not maintainable when a registered, voidable transfer by a natural guardian is not also challenged by a request to set it aside.

issues.legal_issue: A release deed that does not refer to the guardian’s registered sale does not repudiate or avoid that sale.
material_facts: A natural guardian had conveyed the minor’s immovable property by registered sale deeds.
After the minor died before attaining majority, the minor’s mother executed a release deed in favour of the plaintiffs for consideration.
The release deed made no reference to the earlier sales.
No action to set aside the sales was brought within the applicable limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The release deed did not repudiate or avoid the sales, which remained unavoided within the limitation period.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(3) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 makes the specified disposal voidable at the instance of the minor or a person claiming under the minor. A registered sale deed must actually be set aside to remove its legal effect; whether avoidance can occur otherwise than by suit may depend on the facts, but the Court confined its ruling to registered transfers. Article 60 of the Limitation Act, 1963 governs the action to set aside the transfer. The Court relied on Amirtham Kudumbah v. Sarnam Kudumban and Gorakh Nath Dube v. Hari Narain Singh, and distinguished transfers by de facto guardians under Section 11 of the 1956 Act.

rule.if: challenge_to_registered_guardian_transfer and registered_transfer_by_natural_guardian and purported_repudiation_document_omits_transfer and no_timely_action_to_set_aside

predicates.challenge_to_registered_guardian_transfe: The proceeding concerns an attempt by a minor or a person claiming under the minor to avoid a registered transfer made by a guardian.
predicates.registered_transfer_by_natural_guardian: A natural guardian conveyed the minor’s immovable property by registered instrument.
predicates.purported_repudiation_document_omits_tra: The document relied on as repudiation does not refer to the guardian’s transfer.
predicates.no_timely_action_to_set_aside: No action to set aside the registered transfer was brought within the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: A registered transfer by a natural guardian remains unavoided when the relied-on document omits the transfer and no timely action is brought to set it aside.

issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s absolute interest under a bequest following a life estate vests at the testator’s death when the will does not indicate a contrary intention.
material_facts: The will gave the testator’s sons life interests and provided that male heirs of the sons would thereafter take the property absolutely.
The beneficiary’s possession was postponed until after the life interest ended.
The beneficiary was alive when the testator died.
issues.conclusion: The beneficiary’s absolute interest vested on the testator’s death, notwithstanding the postponement of possession until the end of the life estate.
issues.legal_principle: Section 119 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 provides that, unless a contrary intention appears, a legatee’s right to receive a bequest at the proper time becomes vested on the testator’s death even when possession is postponed. Illustration (iii) to Section 119 addresses a fund bequeathed to one person for life and thereafter to another. Sections 19 and 21 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 distinguish vested rights from contingent interests.

predicates.bequest_postpones_possession: The will postpones the beneficiary’s possession of the bequeathed property.
predicates.bequest_grants_absolute_remainder: The will gives the beneficiary an absolute interest after a prior life interest ends.
predicates.no_contrary_intention_appears: The will does not show an intention that the beneficiary’s interest remain unvested until possession becomes available.

issues.definition: When a will postpones possession but grants an absolute remainder without a contrary intention, the remainder interest vests at the testator’s death.
